text: The Computer History Museum (CHM) is located in Mountain View, California, and showcases the stories and artifacts of Silicon Valley and the Information Age, exploring the computing revolution and its societal impact. Its origins trace back to 1968 when Gordon Bell initiated a historical collection effort, coinciding with efforts to preserve the Whirlwind computer; the Museum Project debuted its first exhibit in 1975 in a converted coat closet within a DEC lobby. In 1978, the museum, then known as The Digital Computer Museum (TDCM), moved to a larger DEC lobby in Marlborough, Massachusetts, and opened to the public in September 1979, with Maurice Wilkes delivering the first lecture, a tradition that continues today. TDCM incorporated as The Computer Museum (TCM) in 1982 and relocated to Boston in 1984, settling on Museum Wharf. In 1996/1997, the TCM History Center (TCMHC) was established at Moffett Field, provided by NASA, using an old building formerly housing naval base furniture; a large number of artifacts were transferred from TCM. In 1999, TCMHC incorporated, and TCM ceased operations, shipping its remaining artifacts to TCMHC in 2000. Since the name TCM was retained by the Boston Museum of Science, the center was renamed the Computer History Museum (CHM) in 2000. In 2002, CHM opened its new building at 1401 N. Shoreline Blvd in Mountain View, California, to the public. In 2009, CHM hosted the National Inventors Hall of Fame’s annual induction ceremony, where fifteen inductees were recognized for contributions to semiconductor technology, marking the golden jubilee of the integrated circuit. The facility underwent a two-year $19 million renovation and reopened in January 2011. John Hollar, a former media executive, was appointed CEO in July 2008; Dan'l Lewin, a former technology executive, replaced him as CEO in March 2018; on February 19, 2025, Marc Etkind, former NASA Communications Leader, was appointed as President and Chief Executive Officer. CHM hosts regular public programs under the "CHM Live" banner featuring notable Silicon Valley and global tech leaders, including Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, Reid Hoffman, Elon Musk, and Eric Schmidt, as well as academics and historians, discussing technology’s impact. The museum also organizes special events for key anniversaries, such as the 40th Anniversary of the Apple Macintosh and the 50th Anniversary of Ethernet, with panel discussions on these technologies, and recordings of past events are available on its YouTube channel. CHM hosts TechFest events for families. The museum claims to hold the largest and most significant collection of computing artifacts globally, including a Cray-1, Cray-2, Cray-3, the Utah teapot, the 1969 Neiman Marcus Kitchen Computer, an Apple I, and an early generation of Google’s custom web server racks. The collection includes nearly 90,000 objects, photographs, and films, 4,000 ft (1,200 m) of cataloged documentation, and several hundred gigabytes of software. The CHM oral history program conducts video interviews on computing history, covering computer systems, networking, data-processing, memory, and data-storage, with over 1,000 interviews recorded as of 2021, including panels on the origins of the IBM PC and hard disk drive, and individual interviews with Joanna Hoffman, Steve Chen, Dame Stephanie Shirley, and Donald Knuth. The museum’s 25,000 sq ft (2,300 m²) exhibit "Revolution: The First 2000 Years of Computing," opened on January 13, 2011, spans 20 galleries from the abacus to the Internet and is available online. On January 28, 2017, a 6,000 sq ft (560 m²) exhibit, "Make Software: Change the World!", launched, designed for middle schoolers and older, featuring multimedia and touchscreen interactives, including a software lab for hands-on coding. Other exhibits include a restored PDP-1 minicomputer, two restored IBM 1401 computers, and a restored IBM Ramac 350 disk drive. An operating difference engine designed by Charles Babbage in the 1840s, constructed by the Science Museum of London and on loan from Nathan Myhrvold since 2008, was on display until January 31, 2016. CHM maintains an extensive software collection curated by Al Kossow, a former Apple employee hired in 2006, responsible for preservation and exhibition development; Kossow is also the proprietor of Bitsavers, a large online repository of historical computer manuals and archived software and firmware. In 2010, the museum began collecting source code, starting with Apple’s MacPaint 1.3, available for public download. Subsequent accessions include APL in 2012, Adobe’s Photoshop 1.0.1 in 2013 and Postscript in 2022, Microsoft’s SCP MS-DOS 1.25, Altos MS-DOS 2.11, TeleVideo PC DOS 2.11, and Word for Windows 1.1a under license, and Xerox Alto’s source code released on October 21, 2014, and Apple Lisa’s source code released on January 19, 2023. The Walk-Through Computer exhibit opened on June 23, 1990, featuring a desktop computer, giant monitor, 25-foot keyboard, and 40-inch trackball to control the World Traveler program; it closed on August 5, 1995, and reopened as Walk-Through Computer 2000 on October 21, 1995, with updated features including 3D graphics and the ability to alter pits on a giant CD-ROM visible on a monitor. In 2016, the museum featured a Liquid Galaxy in the "Going Places: A History of Silicon Valley" exhibit, allowing visitors to fly to 20 preselected locations, and also displayed an exhibit on the history of autonomous vehicles from torpedoes to self-driving cars. The CHM Fellow Awards Program honors distinguished technology pioneers for their contributions to computing and the digital age, with the first fellow being Rear Admiral Grace Hopper in 1987; as of 2025, the program has 100 members, and fellow nominations are open to the public year-round.
